transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-10-09
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Ben Kaplan (Redwood AE); Priya Mehta (Redwood SE); Jordan Lee (Redwood Partner Ops); Carlos Ruiz (Whirlwind CTO); Aisha Khan (Whirlwind Head of Cloud Partnerships); Marta Silva (Whirlwind Lead DevOps); Liam O'Connor (Whirlwind Security)

Summary:
Quick partner introduction and discovery between Redwood and Whirlwind Systems. Main goals: validate integration patterns for Whirlwind's SI-led deployment of Redwood into customer environments, clarify private deployment (VPC / on-prem) constraints, discuss GPU vendor preferences and pilot scope, and align on next steps for a technical deep dive and pilot.

Topics covered:
- High-level partner motion and responsibilities
- Private deployment options: VPC vs on-prem box
- GPU vendor compatibility and procurement cadence
- Security, KMS, and audit logging expectations
- Pilot success criteria and timeline

Transcript body:
[00:00:03] Ben (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. Do we have folks on the line from Whirlwind?
[00:00:08] Carlos (Whirlwind): yep hey, Carlos here, thanks Ben. Aisha and Marta and Liam are with me.
[00:00:13] Aisha (Whirlwind): hi hi, thanks for taking the time. We wanted to run through how you typically partner with systems integrators — like how much of the delivery is Redwood vs our SI team.
[00:00:25] Ben (Redwood): totally, that's a great place to start. Quick intro: Redwood generally shows up as the inference runtime + control plane. For SI engagements we tend to do partner enablement (SE workshops), provide the private package for VPC/on-prem, and offer runbooks for network, KMS, and capacity sizing. But the split can be flexible — e.g., your SI can manage provisioning and initial rollout while Redwood owns the runtime upgrades and critical incidents under a partner SLA.
[00:00:50] Priya (Redwood-SE): and to add, we usually do an initial two-day workshop to validate model variants, quantization profiles, and batching configs against the customer's workload. That helps us pin GPU sizing and latency targets.
[00:01:03] Marta (Whirlwind): when you say two-day workshop, is that remote or on-site? And do you bring lab GPUs for benchmarks?
[00:01:10] Priya (Redwood-SE): typically remote with remote access to our test harness. We can occasionally bring a bench kit for on-site but most customers share a sample dataset and we run microbenchmarks against either hosted demo infra or partner-provided GPUs.
[00:01:26] Liam (Whirlwind): from security side I'm curious about the KMS story — we prefer cloud KMS integration and customer-owned keys. Is that supported?
[00:01:34] Ben (Redwood): yes, customer-managed KMS is supported for Private deployments. You can integrate AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or a hardware HSM. We also provide audit logs and can route them to your SI's ELK or to a SI-managed Splunk instance.
[00:01:49] Carlos (Whirlwind): great. Another practical question: Whirlwind has customers who are on-prem only — do you have an on-prem appliance or is it a VM/container package?
[00:01:57] Priya (Redwood-SE): it's a packaged private deployment — containerized runtime plus a lightweight control plane. For fully air-gapped customers we have an on-prem bundle and offline installer. There are some limitations on autoscaling and telemetry in air-gapped mode; we'll document those.
[00:02:15] Carlos (Whirlwind): okay noted. On the GPU side, who do you certify? We have procurement agreements with a few GPU vendors — we need to know compatibility.
[00:02:24] Jordan (Redwood-PartnerOps): we maintain a model-hardware compatibility matrix. Short answer: we support mainstream NVIDIA Ampere and Hopper families, and are working to expand support for Arm/Ascend and some third-party accelerators. For partners we can share a matrix that maps model families to recommended GPU SKUs and quantization profiles.
[00:02:42] Marta (Whirlwind): do you have any preferences on drivers or orchestrators? Our standard is k8s plus a GPU operator.
[00:02:48] Priya (Redwood-SE): k8s with GPU operator is our common path. We can also do bare-metal deployments with our runtime manager. We have tested with NGC drivers and some custom stacks — there can be variance in performance so the workshop helps pin that.
[00:03:03] Aisha (Whirlwind): on partner economics — do you do revenue share for SI-led deals or is it referral only?
[00:03:09] Ben (Redwood): we have a couple of partner models: referral, reseller, and strategic partner programs. For SI-led deals we usually offer reseller discounts or partner commission tiers depending on volume and committed reserved capacity. Jordan can follow up with the partner contract template.
[00:03:24] Jordan (Redwood-PartnerOps): yep I'll share the partner playbook and the partner rate card after this call.
[00:03:29] Carlos (Whirlwind): perfect. Also, our clients frequently ask about latency SLOs for chat vs embeddings — do you publish typical numbers?
[00:03:38] Priya (Redwood-SE): we publish benchmark profiles for each model variant. Embeddings are usually single-request low-latency; chat depends on sequence length and KV caching. For quantized medium-size models we've seen 20–60ms per token on A100 like instances in batch sizes typical for interactive chat. But again depends on prompt length and batching.
[00:03:59] Liam (Whirlwind): can you explain KV cache and how that affects throughput when multiple tenants share a dedicated pool?
[00:04:06] Priya (Redwood-SE): sure — KV cache is per-session and is critical for auto-regressive models to avoid re-computing full context. In multi-tenant pools we do session-aware routing and can pin model variants to capacity pools to reduce cold-starts. We also have prefix caching and optional per-customer kv caches for dedicated clusters.
[00:04:26] Marta (Whirlwind): for networking, will you require outbound access to Redwood control plane? Some clients are strict.
[00:04:32] Ben (Redwood): for Private deployments we can operate with a minimal control plane footprint — some customers want a fully private control plane; others allow periodic telemetry egress. We support both: fully isolated on-prem or VPC peering to a private control plane endpoint in your account. We'll capture that per-customer in the runbook.
[00:04:52] Carlos (Whirlwind): what about upgrade windows and rollback? Our SI engagements have tight SLAs.
[00:04:58] Priya (Redwood-SE): we do canary rollouts and support canary + automatic fallback. For private deployments we recommend staged upgrades with a snapshot and KV cache warm-up plan. Rollback is supported but must be coordinated for stateful caches.
[00:05:12] Aisha (Whirlwind): good. Let's talk pilot scope — what's a reasonable timeline for a partner-led pilot to validate model quality and latency?
[00:05:20] Ben (Redwood): from kickoff to first benchmarks: 2–3 weeks typically. That includes access to a test account, sample prompts, and running our eval harness. If you want on-prem GPUs involved it can stretch to 3–6 weeks depending on procurement and access.
[00:05:33] Marta (Whirlwind): procurement is often the blocker. We need an initial GPU SKU recommendation so we can fast-track short-term rentals.
[00:05:40] Priya (Redwood-SE): we'll send a quick GPU sizing checklist after the call — it has recommended SKUs for common latencies and throughput targets, including recommended batch sizes and mem footprints.
[00:05:50] Liam (Whirlwind): one more security question — do you support customer-side logging redaction? we have PII concerns, and often the SI has to add a redaction layer before logs land in central store.
[00:05:59] Ben (Redwood): yes, we support configurable log redaction and granular audit logs with event types. For highly regulated customers we can disable detailed telemetry and provide periodic aggregated metrics instead.
[00:06:12] Carlos (Whirlwind): competitors — are there any gotchas where CloudRunX or AzuraML do something different that we should know when positioning?
[00:06:19] Jordan (Redwood-PartnerOps): CloudRunX tends to couple model hosting with their cloud storage tightly which is nice for quick startups but limits flexibility. AzuraML offers managed private endpoints but their cost for high-throughput workloads can be higher. Our pitch is unified runtime flexibility + partner enablement and predictable costs for sustained inference.
[00:06:37] Aisha (Whirlwind): ok that's helpful. For pilot acceptance criteria — from our side the customer will want: latency under X for 95th pct, feature parity with current model outputs, and reproducible inference results. Can Redwood produce a test harness and baseline report?
[00:06:49] Priya (Redwood-SE): yes we have an eval harness that runs closed prompts, A/B comparisons and produces a results pack with latency percentiles, token-level cost, and output-diff stats. We'll generate a baseline against your sample prompts.
[00:07:03] Marta (Whirlwind): how do you handle secrets and envs in private deploys if the SI manages infra? we want to avoid embedding creds in templates.
[00:07:11] Ben (Redwood): recommended pattern is to integrate with the customer's KMS or a partner-managed secrets store. Our deployment manifests reference secrets via injection hooks and never store keys in plain text. We'll share the manifest patterns.
[00:07:24] Liam (Whirlwind): do you support SAML SSO to the Redwood console for customer admins?
[00:07:28] Priya (Redwood-SE): yes SAML and SSO are supported. For Private we can tie into your IdP and support role-based access controls.
[00:07:35] Ben (Redwood): quick note — we should capture the high-level responsibilities: Whirlwind/SI will own procurement, hardware staging, and infra patching unless Redwood is contracted for dedicated ops. Redwood will own runtime patches, model onboarding, and the eval harness. We'll put this in the partner playbook.
[00:07:52] Carlos (Whirlwind): makes sense. Anything we should be aware of re: licensing or export controls for specific model families?
[00:07:59] Priya (Redwood-SE): license and model vetting is part of onboarding; some models have restricted commercial use or export rules — we'll surface that per model in the catalog.
[00:08:09] Aisha (Whirlwind): can you share a sample customer runbook so we can see the level of detail?
[00:08:13] Ben (Redwood): yes — action item: we'll send the runbook template plus partner integration diagram.
[00:08:18] -- conversation continues with clarifications and some interruptions --
[00:25:02] [roughly midway, technical deep-dive starting]
[00:25:06] Priya (Redwood-SE): for the deep dive next week we'll want network diagrams, sample prompt set, and a list of top models you're evaluating. We'll try to run a quick microbenchmark for an LLM-7B variant and a 13B variant to show delta in latency and cost.
[00:25:21] Marta (Whirlwind): we can pull those together. Also our customers often want to see per-token cost numbers; can you provide a ballpark?
[00:25:28] Priya (Redwood-SE): ballpark will depend on GPU SKU, batch size, and quantization. For a quantized 7B on T4-class it's X cents per 1k tokens, on A100 it's lower per token but higher fixed infra. We'll send a sample cost comparison spreadsheet.
[00:25:44] Liam (Whirlwind): for the pilot, do you need customer production data or can we anonymize and use synthetic prompts?
[00:25:50] Ben (Redwood): synthetic prompts are fine for initial perf. For quality/eval we prefer a small anonymized prompt set. If you need guidance on anonymization we can share a script.
[00:26:02] Carlos (Whirlwind): ok great. timeline again?
[00:26:06] Ben (Redwood): we'll aim to get the partner docs and GPU checklist out today/tomorrow, schedule the SE deep dive for next week, and start provisioning test resources within 2–3 days of privacy approvals.
[00:26:16] Aisha (Whirlwind): sounds good. Any major risks we should call out?
[00:26:20] Jordan (Redwood-PartnerOps): common risks: procurement lead time, network egress approvals for telemetry, and model licensing for certain enterprise models. We'll flag these in the runbook.
[00:26:29] Carlos (Whirlwind): cool. Liam, anything from security?
[00:26:32] Liam (Whirlwind): just that we'll want the SOC2 docs and details about key lifecycle management. If Redwood can provide an HSM integration diagram that's helpful.
[00:26:41] Ben (Redwood): we'll attach the SOC2 and HSM notes in the security pack.
[00:26:44] -- wrapping up --
[00:39:10] Ben (Redwood): recap: Priya will draft the GPU sizing checklist; Jordan will share partner playbook and rate card; Ben will send the runbook and partner integration diagram; Marta and Carlos will share infra diagrams and prompts; Liam will list KMS/compliance constraints. We'll plan the SE deep dive next week, tentatively Wednesday.
[00:39:32] Aisha (Whirlwind): thanks everyone. That timeline works for us.
[00:39:36] Carlos (Whirlwind): thanks, talk soon.
[00:39:40] Priya (Redwood-SE): thanks all, bye.

End of call
